summary:
Jeju stands under South Korea's national framework. South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, a provision the Constitutional Court upheld in 2023 after a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available on Jeju and the surgery requirement has fallen. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that conditioning gender change on surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change nationwide, including on Jeju, and the wire report records no specific case on the island. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. A person transitioning from male to female who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 was advised by police to avoid women's public restrooms; the Seoul Central District Court ruled on 2 July 2024 that this advice infringed personal rights, and on 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal, finalising 300,000 won in damages against a 3 million won claim. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% avoided facilities out of fear, and a 2021 damages award compensated a student barred from academy restrooms. These national rulings govern Jeju, where the reporting describes no specific incident.

Protection machinery on the ground is thin. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling extending same-sex partners a measure of recognition in healthcare.

For a visitor on the ground, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but organised conservative opposition is active and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources, and nothing locally reported makes Jeju safer or harsher than the national picture.
tangentialFactors:
Two official signals pull in opposite directions for a trans visitor. Courts have repeatedly ordered the state to pay damages over restroom access and have removed surgery as a condition of legal recognition, while the executive branch declined in November 2023 to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients and the legislature has never passed an anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

Exclusion from military service sits alongside criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct within the armed forces, so a visitor who is of service age and openly trans may encounter a legal regime that treats gender non-conformity as disqualifying even where civilian life is lawful.

Organised conservative opposition is a documented feature of the social environment, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report documents persistent discrimination against LGBT people while also recording a comparatively strong position for free media and civil society, which means incidents are more likely to be reported and contested than concealed.

Facility avoidance is a widespread reported behaviour rather than an isolated fear: 41% of 591 transgender respondents to a 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey avoided facilities out of fear, and a 2021 award compensated a student excluded from academy restrooms. A visitor should expect self-restriction of restroom use to be a common local strategy even where the law is on their side.

Jeju has no locally documented incident in these sources, positive or negative. The island's position is inherited from national rulings rather than from any local enforcement record, so a visitor should read Seoul-based neighbourhood conditions as indicative of the wider national climate rather than as a description of Jeju itself.
localsOnly:
Residents on Jeju can apply to change registered sex without having undergone sex-reassignment surgery, following the 8 May 2024 Yeongdong ruling that removed the surgical prerequisite nationwide and demoted the older judicial guidelines requiring surgery to reference status. The Supreme Court has also permitted a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Residents who are told by police to avoid public restrooms have a enforceable claim: the Seoul Central District Court held on 2 July 2024 that such advice infringes personal rights and that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right, and the Seoul appellate court finalised 300,000 won in damages against the state on 22 July 2024 after the state's appeal was dismissed.

Recourse for residents is limited to individual litigation and complaints to the National Human Rights Commission of Korea. Employment, accommodation and access to services carry no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, because no comprehensive anti-discrimination law exists.

Transgender residents face documented barriers in hospitalisation. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospital care after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, arguing that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Transgender people are barred from military service, and consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel remains a criminal offence under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 with a penalty of up to two years' imprisonment, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023.

Residents in same-sex partnerships have no access to marriage. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling extended a measure of recognition to same-sex partners in healthcare, and nothing further on partner status is established in these sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a specific incident involving a trans visitor or resident on Jeju, so the island's practical conditions remain unresolved rather than confirmed as benign or hostile.

Whether the restroom ruling's reasoning is applied consistently by courts outside Seoul is not sourced here; the two decisions cited sit in Seoul and Yeongdong, and no Jeju court decision on facilities appears in the inventory.

Hate-crime protection for gender identity or expression is not addressed by any source provided, and the absence of a general anti-discrimination statute leaves the existence of any narrower protective provision unresolved.

Local healthcare availability for trans patients on Jeju, including hormone therapy continuity and willingness of private clinics to admit trans inpatients, is not sourced. The only healthcare evidence is the national-level November 2023 exchange between the National Human Rights Commission of Korea and the Ministry of Health and Welfare.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender documents is not covered by these sources, so how a foreign passport with an amended or inconsistent gender marker is handled on arrival at Jeju is unresolved.

The scope of the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights beyond healthcare, and whether it affects taxation, inheritance or hospital visitation for a visiting partner, is not established here.
